PART `I BENZOIC ACID AND ITS SALTS

0.

FOREWORD

0.1 This Indian Standard ( Part 1 1 was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 30 October 1956, after the draft finalized by the Food Hygiene Sectional Committee had been approved by the Agricultural and Food Products Division Council.

0.2 Far pro_tecting foad from microibial detarioqtion, a number of methods, such as application of heat or cold, dehydration, fermentation, irradiation or addition of certain chemicals, are employed. Besides extending the period of use of a food, a chemical prcrservatlve should be safe for hum:zn consumption, should not impart undesirable arganoleptic changes, be economical in use and be capable of being analysed. While the use of chemical preservatives to be safe under conJitions of use is governed by law, it is considered necessary to prescribe methods for their analysis. The use of these methods would not only ensure repeatable and reproducible results for their correct interpretation, but would also facilitate inter-laboratory comparison. 0.3 The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 19.54 and the Rules framed thereunder allow the use of two classes of preservatives, class I and class 11. Class I preservatives include common salt, sugar, dextrose, glucose ( syrup >$ wood smoke, spices, vinegar acetic acid, honey, etc. Class 11 preservatives include inorganic substances, such as sulphurous acid including salts thereof, nitrates of sodium or potassium and organic substances like benzoic acid including salts thereof, sorbic acid including its sodium, potassium and calcium salts and sodium and calcium propion&. 0.4 This standard, covering the determination of organic preservatives, is king iss~led in three parts. This part ( Part 1) covers the determination of benzoic acid and its salts in foodstuffs. Part 2 covers propionic asid and it% salts and Part 3 covers sorbic acid and its salts. 0.5 Bs~zoic acid and its salts are commonly used as a preservative in asn-alcoholic wines, squashes, crushes, fruit syrups, cordials, fruit 3

IS : 12014 ( Part 1) - 1986

juices, barley water, sweetened mineral water, iam. marmalade, canned cherry, fruit jelly, pickles and chulneys made from fruit or vegetables, tomato and other sauces, syrups and SHARBATS. 0.6 In reporting the result of a test or analysjs made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be d6ne in accordance with 1S : 2-19hO*.

5.2.1 General Food Stuffs - Weigh accurately about 150 g of the material, ground if necessary, in a suitable digestor and add to it about

*Specification for rectified spirit ( revised).

Digest the material 300 ml of the saturated sodium chloride solution. and then add 15 g of pulverized sodium chloride. Make the solution alkaline to litmus by adding required amount of calcium hydroxide solution. Transfer the solution to a 500-ml volumetric flask and make up to volume with saturated solution of sodium chloride. Allow it to stand for at least two hours shaking frequently; centrifuge, if necessary, and filter. 5.2.2 Catsup - Weigh accurately about 150 g of the sample and add to it 15 g pulverised sodium chloride and transfer the mixture to a 500-ml volumetric flask rinsing with 150 ml saturated sodium chloride solution. Make slightly alkaline to litmus paper with IO percent sodium hydroxide solution and dilute to volume with saturated sodium chloride solution. Allow it to stand for 2 hours shaking frequently centrifuge, if necessary and filter. 5.2.3 Jellies, Jams, Preserves and Marmalades - Weigh accurately 150 g sample and digest in 300 ml of saturated sodium chloride solution. Add 15 g pulverised sodium chloride and make alkaline to litmus paper with calcium hydroxide solution. Transfer the solution to a 500 ml volumetric flask and make up to volume with saturated sodium chloride Allow it to stand for two hours shaking frequently centrifuge, solution. if necessary and filter. 5.2.4 Cider Containing Alcohol and Similar Products - Accurately weigh 250 g sample, make it alkaline to litmus paper with 10 percent sodium hyd'roxide solution and evaporate on steam bath to 100 ml. Transfer the solution to a 250 ml volumetric flask, add 30 g pulverised sodium chloride and shake until dissolved. Dilute to volume with saturated sodium chloride solution. Allow it to stand for two hours, shaking frequently, centrifuge, if necessary and filter. 5.2.5 Salted or Dried Fish - Accurately weigh 50 g of sample and Transfer the sample into a 500 ml volumetric flask with a little amount of distilled water. Make the solution slightly alkaline to litmus paper with 10 percent sodium hydroxide solution and dilute to volume with distilled water. Allow it to stand for atleast 2 hours shaking frequently, centrifuge, ifnecessary and filter. Pipette 300 ml of the filtrate into another 500 ml volumetric flask and add 90 g of pulverised sodium chloride. Shake until sodium chloride dissolves and dilute to volume with saturated sodium chloride solution. Mix tboroughly and filter off the precipitated protein and other extraneous matter.
grind it.

A natural hygroscopic reagent like calcium chloride may be used for Avoid drawing off the aqueous layer. breaking the emulsion. 5,3.2 Transfer the extract to a porcelain dish rinse the container the several times with a small quantity of chloroform, and evapor-ate at room temperature in a current of dry air. Alternatively, transfer it into an Erlenmeyet flask and distil slowly to one-quarter of its volume. Transfer it to the dish, rinsing the flask with small amounts of chloroform and evaporate to dryness at room temperature in a current of dry air. Dry the residue overnight in a desiccator containing concentrated sulphuric acid.

6.311.3 Solid products - Cut a portion of the sample for analysis Take about 40 g of the prointo small pieces and remove the stones. duct and crush them in a homgenizer or a mortar. 6.3.2 Test Portion
6.3.2.1 Liquid products - Take 20 ml of the prepared sample free from suspended matters with the help of the pipette, mix them with about 50 ml of distilled water and transfer them to a 500-m] separating funnel. In the case of pulpy liquid products, place 20 ml of the prgduct, in a mortar and dilute them with 20 ml of distilled water. After decant&ion, filter the liquid. The residue is dissolved twice with 20 ml of water. The filtrates are directly collected in the separating funnel.

6.3.212 Thick or tolid products - Weigh to the nearest 0'01 g, about 10 g of the prepared sample. Entrain in a 250-ml borosilicate' glass flask with ground-glass stopper with 30 to 40 ml of distilled water; add about 50 mg of monosodium carhonate ( see Note >, shake and place on a waterbath at 70 to 80�C for I5 to 30 minutes. Pour the contents of the flask on a fluted filter paper and rinse twice with 15 to 20 ml of distilled water. The filtrate and the washings are collected in a 500-ml seperq tilag funnel. Allow to cool.

carbonate NOTE - The purpose of adding monosodium acid, the traces of which could be lost by volatilization. is to salify the benzoic

6.3.2.3 Extraction of the benzoic acid - Introduce 1 g of tartaris acid into the separating funnel containing the aqueous drlution of the product to be analysed, add 60 ml of diethyl ether and shake carefully.

Allow to settle and then collect the ether layer in another separaWash the aqueous phase in the first funnel a second time ting funnel. with 60 ml of diethyl ether. Allow to settle and add once again the ether layer `to the first one. Carry out in the sa~me manner a third extraction with 30 ml of diethyl ether. Add successively 10 ml, then 5 ml of sodium hydroxide solution and two sets of 10 ml of distilled water to the combined ether extract. Shake and after allowing to settle down, collect the aqueous phases in a dish. Place the dish on water-bath until about half of the alkaline solution is evaporated so as to eliminate the dissolved diethyl ether. cooling, transfer the con6.3.2.4 Purification of benzoic acid -After tents of the dish to a 250-ml flask with a ground-glass stopper contaiuing a mixture of 20 ml of. dilute sulphuric acid and 20 ml of potassium dichromate solution. Stopper the flask, shake and allow to remain in contact for at least an hour.
NOTE 1 - The extension of the time of this oxidation does not create any difficulty because the benzoic acid withstands this oxidizing mixture.

also contains sorbic acid it is necessary NOTE 2 - When the original product to extend by 24 hours the oxidation in order to ensure the complete elimination of this anti-fungal agent.

6.3.2.5 Preparation of the ether solution - Extract the benzoic acid by treating twice the chromic solution with 20 to 25 ml of diethyl ether and collecting the ether solutions. Wash the ether solution twice with a few millilitres of distilled water. After carefully decanting on a dry filter paper, collect the filtrate in a SO-ml volumetric flask. Wash the filter with a few millilitres of diethyl ether so as to bring the filtrate to50ml. *

6.3.2.7 Potting of the calibration curbe - Into a series of six 50 ml volumeteric Aasks, iatroduce 5, 7'5, 10, 12'5, 15 and 20 ml of the standard solution of benzoic acid. Make up the volume to 50 ml with diethyl ether. The solutions obtained contain 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 40 pg of benzoic acid per litre. Carry out on these solutions the differential measurements by proceeding as indicated in 6.3.2.6. Plot the curve giving the differential measurements as a function of the number of micrograms of benzoic acid per litre indicated above.
